content: Brain tumors are among the most challenging cancers to diagnose because their symptoms, such as headaches, cognitive impairments, and seizures, are often more commonly associated with less serious conditions. To address this, various interventions have been proposed to reduce the time it takes to diagnose brain tumors. These include national awareness campaigns, streamlined diagnostic pathways, and protocols designed to identify brain tumors based on a patient’s symptoms and clinical signs. Additionally, efforts to reduce waiting times for brain imaging have been suggested. If these interventions successfully shorten the time to diagnosis, they could potentially prevent clinical deterioration in patients and open up a wider range of treatment options. The objective of this review was to systematically assess the evidence on the effectiveness of interventions aimed at encouraging symptomatic individuals to seek medical attention earlier (reducing the patient interval), lowering the threshold for primary care referrals (reducing the primary care interval), and expediting the time to imaging and diagnosis (reducing the secondary care and overall diagnostic intervals). Furthermore, the review aimed to provide a brief economic commentary summarizing the cost-effectiveness of these interventions. To gather evidence on effectiveness, the researchers searched databases including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase for studies published between January 2000 and January 2020. They also reviewed ClinicalTrials.gov up to May 2020 and examined conference proceedings from 2014 to 2018. For economic evidence, they searched the UK National Health Services Economic Evaluation Database for studies published between 2000 and December 2014. The review intended to include studies that evaluated any active intervention influencing the diagnostic pathway, such as clinical guidelines, direct access to imaging, public health campaigns, educational programs, or other strategies aimed at the early detection of primary brain tumors. Both randomized and non-randomized comparative studies were eligible for inclusion, and the review was open to participants of all ages presenting with symptoms suggestive of a brain tumor. Two independent reviewers assessed the titles and abstracts identified through the search strategy, as well as the full texts of potentially relevant studies. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer if necessary. However, the review did not identify any studies that met the inclusion criteria. A total of 115 studies were excluded, primarily due to their study design, which often lacked control groups. No economic evidence was found to support a brief economic commentary on the cost-effectiveness of these interventions. In conclusion, this review did not find any high-quality studies that provided evidence on the effectiveness or cost-effectiveness of strategies to reduce the time to diagnosis of brain tumors. This is despite the fact that early diagnosis of brain tumors was identified as a research priority by the James Lind Alliance in 2015. The findings underscore the urgent need for well-designed research in this area to identify effective strategies for improving the timely diagnosis of brain tumors.
